newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Militant S.Korean union slams draft labour bill.
newsitem.headline: Militant S.Korean union slams draft labour bill.

text.p: South Korea's outlawed union organisation on Sunday denounced a new version of a controversial labour law, slated to be submitted to parliament on Monday, and vowed further industrial action if it was passed.

The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said it would fight the law's passage, even though the revised bill will delay for two years a controversial clause which allows companies to lay off workers, a provision which sparked worker fury.
"There's not much difference between the original bill and the new one," senior confederation official Chung Sung-hee said in an interview.
"We will launch campaigns to disobey clauses that we think are inappropriate."
"And we will continue labour action until parliament comes up with a more acceptable bill," Chung said.
Protests would include nationwide rallies, the group said. Unions would also link opposition to the new legislation to negotiations over annual pay increases that usually begin in April.

President Kim Young-sam was forced to return the original bill to parliament after its forced passage with no debate last December sparked almost four weeks of labour strikes that cost the nation $3.28 billion in lost production and $509 million in lost exports.

An all-party parliamentary committee cobbled together a compromise on most points on Saturday after missing a deadline a week earlier. A parliamentary spokesman said the draft would be submitted to the National Assembly for a vote on Monday.
The new bill puts back by two years a key concession to employers making it easier for them to shed staff.
Layoffs are all but impossible in South Korea, where redundancies must be approved by a court.
The new draft would also legalise multiple union organisations at a national level, but workers would have to choose a single union to represent them at a company level for another five years.
This would break the monopoly of the Korean Federation of Trade Unions.

International labour organisations, and South Korea's fellow members of the Organisation for Economic Planning and Development, condemned the old law for maintaining a ban on free trade union association until 2000.
The ban was a spillover from the days of military-backed authoritarian rule.
Kim had earlier insisted a flexible labour market was essential to improve the country's industrial competitiveness and reduce a worrying trade deficit.
Other clauses in the new law would tip the balance of industrial power away from unions, which began flexing their muscles with the advent of democracy in the late 1980s.

It upholds the principle of "no work no pay" for striking workers, requires the abolition of salary payments by companies to full-time union officials in five years, and permits flexible working hours.
Chung said flexible hours would "allow firms to exploit workers, and the 'no work no pay' provision would deter unions from going on strike".
He said abolishing salary payments to full-time union officials was unacceptable.
The Federation of Korean Industries, a lobbying group for the nation's huge business conglomerates or "chaebol", offered a grudging welcome to the blueprint on Saturday.
